conservation-cosmology.title: Conservation in Cosmology
conservation-cosmology.content:
Energy conservation in an expanding spacetime operates under the covariant conservation of the stress-energy tensor, which accounts for the geometric stretching of the background metric. This thermodynamic evolution, which governs the expansion histories of different cosmic species, contrasts with the static halo boundaries that parameterize the Density Profiles of Dark Matter. In the standard Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric, the conservation laws require that the local changes in energy density are coupled to the work done by pressure against the expansion coordinate grids. The physical description of this energy evolution is formally modeled by the continuity relation known as The Fluid Equation, which relates the time-derivative of the density \( \dot{\rho} \) to the pressure \( P \) and the Hubble parameter \( H = \dot{a}/a \) as

\[ \dot{\rho} + 3H \left( \rho + \frac{P}{c^2} \right) = 0 \]

where the expansion parameter acts as a friction-like term, guaranteeing that relativistic species lose energy faster than pressureless matter. This dynamic density evolution governs how global background structures evolve, whereas local departures from this smooth expansion are mapped by the non-zero Peculiar Velocities of galaxies and the hierarchical cluster systems that form around them.

The mathematical origin of this conservation law is rooted in the Noether theorem, which links spatial translation symmetries to momentum conservation and time translation symmetries to energy conservation. In a dynamically expanding universe, the explicit time-dependence of the metric tensor \( g_{\mu\nu}(t) \) breaks global time-translation invariance, meaning that the total energy of the universe is not conserved in the classical sense. The kinematics of the cosmic fluid components are governed by the relativistic Energy-Momentum Relation \( E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2 \), where the photon momentum \( p_\gamma \) decays as \( a^{-1} \) due to cosmological redshift. For relativistic particles with zero rest mass \( m_0 = 0 \), the energy density \( \rho_r \) decreases as \( a^{-4} \), whereas for non-relativistic baryons, the mass-energy density \( \rho_m \) is conserved in a comoving volume, decaying strictly as \( a^{-3} \). This difference in decay rates arises because the physical volume increases as the cube of the scale factor while the photon wavelength is stretched by a single power of the scale factor.

The thermodynamic consequence of this scale-dependent decay is that the universe transitioned from a radiation-dominated era to a matter-dominated era, and eventually to the current dark energy-dominated epoch. Throughout these transitions, the evolution of the spatial metric is tracked by The Scale Factor a(t), which maps the physical coordinate distance \( d(t) = a(t) x \) relative to the comoving coordinate \( x \). The empirical verification of these cosmological conservation scaling laws is a major objective for modern astronomical observatories. The high-precision weak lensing and baryon acoustic oscillation surveys planned for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will measure the growth of cosmic structures with a precision of \( \sigma_8 \le 0.01 \), verifying if dark energy behaves strictly as a static cosmological constant \( w = -1 \) or a dynamical field that violates classical energy conservation. By observing millions of distant galaxies across a wide range of redshifts \( 0.5 \le z \le 2.0 \), these cosmological observations will map the evolution of the spatial metric and constrain any potential energy exchange between dark matter and dark energy.

A clear demonstration of the limiting case for this cosmological energy conservation relation occurs in the limit of local, flat Minkowski spacetime, or as the cosmological scale factor remains static. As the scale factor \( a(t) \) approaches a constant value \( a_0 \), the Hubble expansion rate \( H \) vanishes, and the explicit time-dependence of the metric tensor is eliminated. Under this static-space limit, the non-linear cosmological fluid continuity equation simplifies smoothly to the standard conservation equations of flat space, where the time-derivative of the energy density vanishes entirely \( \partial \rho / \partial t = 0 \) in the absence of local thermodynamic gradients. Consequently, the highly scale-dependent, redshift-driven energy decay of the expanding universe dissolves into the flat-space regularities of classical energy conservation, proving that the cosmological conservation model is fully compatible with classical physics. This seamless mathematical transition guarantees that the flat-space limit is recovered without any coordinate singularities, preserving the thermodynamic consistency of physical models across all scales. Under this continuous reduction, the non-linear redshift-driven density decay phases contract into static, local energy conservation profiles that are observed in isolated, non-expanding laboratory systems.

identities.description: The fluid continuity equation models local energy-momentum conservation under a Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker expanding metric.

big-bang-theory.title: The Big Bang
big-bang-theory.content:
Cosmological expansion from an initial high-density, high-temperature singularity governs the global geometry and thermal history of our universe. This evolutionary framework, which establishes a singular beginning approximately \( 13.8 \text{ billion years} \) ago, provides the physical context for mapping the cosmic distance scale. In contrast to local distance indicators calibrated through the Geometric Basis of Parallax to measure stellar positions within \( d \le 10 \text{ kpc} \), the global metric expansion is tracked by the cosmological redshift of standard candles. On galactic scales, the massive potential wells that shape the hierarchical assembly of galaxies are modeled by The Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) Profile, representing the dark matter distributions that grew from the tiny density seeds \( \delta \approx 10^{-5} \) generated during the initial expansion epoch.

The dynamics of this expanding spatial metric are governed by the general relativistic field equations, which relate the curvature of spacetime to the energy-momentum density of the cosmic fluid. Under this framework, the deceleration or acceleration of the scale factor \( a(t) \) is determined by the total energy density \( \rho \) and pressure \( P \) of the universal components. The expansion rate of this uniform cosmic metric is formally modeled by the second Friedmann equation, which incorporates the cosmological constant \( \Lambda \) as

\[ \frac{\ddot{a}}{a} = -\frac{4\pi G}{3} \left( \rho + \frac{3P}{c^2} \right) + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3} \]

where the acceleration \( \ddot{a} \) depends on the gravitational attraction of matter and the repulsive pressure of dark energy, guaranteeing that the expansion rate transitions from decelerating to accelerating as the scale factor increases. This relation ensures that the global dynamics are determined by the local equation of state \( w = P/\rho c^2 \) of the dominant cosmic fluid.

The thermodynamic history of the expanding universe couples the propagation of matter and radiation to the general relativistic The Stress-Energy Tensor (\(T_{\mu\nu}\)), which describes the distribution of energy and momentum in spacetime. The physical properties of these interacting species are governed by the relativistic Energy-Momentum Relation \( E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2 \), where the momentum vector \( p^\mu \) of the particles decays purely geometrically due to the expansion. In the high-density primordial era, the extreme thermal pressure prevents any gravitational collapse, whereas in cold, dead remnants, The Stability Limit of Degenerate Stars is determined by the Fermi pressure of degenerate electrons or neutrons. This high-density stability limit represents the final state of stellar structures, contrasting with the early universe where high densities were accompanied by extreme temperatures and dynamical expansion.

The primordial nucleosynthesis that occurred in the first three minutes of expansion set the chemical composition of the universe, producing approximately 75% hydrogen and 25% helium, with trace amounts of lithium. This primordial abundance ratio \( Y_p \approx 0.25 \) serves as the chemical starting point for all subsequent stellar generations, setting the initial conditions for stellar birth. The subsequent formation of stars and galaxies is governed by the relation between the Initial Mass and Stellar Evolution, where the mass of a progenitor star determines its lifetime and nucleosynthetic output. By measuring the low metallicity \( [Fe/H] \le -3 \) of the oldest population III stars, astronomers can trace the chemical enrichment history back to the primordial gas, verifying the predictions of the standard expansion model governed by the expansion parameter \( H_0 \).

A clear demonstration of the limiting case for this expansion relation occurs in the limit of local, small-scale gravitationally bound systems, or as the spatial separation between objects approaches zero relative to the cosmic horizon. As the physical distance \( r \) between two massive bodies decreases, the local gravitational attraction \( F_g = G M_1 M_2 / r^2 \) dominates over the expansion force of the cosmological metric. Under this bound-system limit, the general relativistic Friedmann expansion equations simplify smoothly to the standard Newtonian equations of motion, where the cosmological expansion rate \( H \) plays an entirely negligible role in the local dynamics. Consequently, the highly dynamical, expanding metric of the universe dissolves into the flat-space regularities of classical Newtonian gravity, proving that the Big Bang model is fully compatible with local classical mechanics. This seamless mathematical transition guarantees that the flat-space limit is recovered without any physical or coordinate singularities, preserving the dynamic consistency of cosmological models across all spatial scales. Under this continuous reduction, the non-linear cosmological expansion phases contract into static, local Newtonian orbits.

wave-particle-duality.title: Wave-Particle Duality
wave-particle-duality.content:
The co-existence of wave-like and particle-like properties in quantum entities challenges the classical dichotomies of physics, requiring a probabilistic description of physical systems. This fundamental duality, which manifests when a coherent beam of particles propagates through a double-slit aperture, is characterized by the formation of an interference or Diffraction Pattern on a detecting screen. In contrast to classical waves where intensity is continuously distributed, the diffraction pattern is constructed by the discrete, point-like arrivals of individual particles over time. The particle-like energy transport of these quanta is demonstrated by the photoelectric effect, where the kinetic energy of ejected electrons is measured using the Stopping Potential and Retarding Fields \( V_0 \) necessary to reduce the electric current to zero, revealing a linear dependence on frequency \( E = h u \) where the Planck constant \( h \) acts as the quantum of action.

The physical description of these dual behaviors is rooted in the formulation of quantum mechanics, where physical states are represented as vectors in a Hilbert space. Under this framework, the quantum description of particles and fields does not rely on a fixed, pre-existing spatial background, but is formulated in a way that respects Background Independence, where the geometry of space is dynamical and coupled to the quantum states. The transition from classical trajectories to quantum wavefields is mathematically described by the path integral formulation, where the probability amplitude \( K(x_f, t_f; x_i, t_i) \) is a sum over all possible paths, each weighted by a phase factor \( e^{i S / \hbar} \) determined by the classical action \( S \).

The probabilistic interpretation of these interference patterns bridges the gap between individual quantum events and macroscopic statistical distributions. The connection between the probability density of a single quantum measurement and the long-term relative frequency of outcomes is formally modeled by the principles of Frequentist Statistics in Quantum Mechanics. In this statistical framework, the probability \( P(x) \, dx \) of finding a particle in a spatial interval is defined as the limit of the relative frequency as the number of independent measurements \( N \) approaches infinity. This statistical regularity guarantees that the seemingly random, individual particle impacts compile over many trials into the continuous, wave-like interference profiles predicted by the wave equation with spatial coordinates \( x \).

The wave properties of massive particles are not restricted to photons but represent a universal characteristic of all matter, including electrons, neutrons, and large molecules. The propagation of these Matter Waves is governed by the de Broglie relations, which mathematically link the momentum of a particle to its spatial wavelength. The physical existence of these waves is demonstrated by electron diffraction experiments in crystals, where the constructive interference of electron waves occurs at specific angles \( \theta \) governed by Bragg's law \( 2d \sin\theta = n\lambda \). This wave-like propagation ensures that massive particles exhibit diffraction and interference effects that are entirely analogous to those of electromagnetic radiation with wavelength \( \lambda \).

The mathematical representation of a quantum entity's state is encapsulated by its wave function, which contains all the physical information accessible through measurement. The relation between the spatial distribution and the corresponding momentum state is formally modeled by the Fourier transform of the state, which maps The Wave Function and Probability Amplitudes \( \psi(x) \) to its momentum-space representation \( \phi(p) \). The probability of finding the particle with momentum \( p \) is given by the square of the momentum-space amplitude \( |\phi(p)|^2 \), demonstrating the continuous transition between position and momentum descriptions. This dual representation represents the mathematical basis of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle \( \Delta x \, \Delta p \ge \hbar/2 \), which forbids the simultaneous, precise determination of both variables.

A clear demonstration of the limiting case for this wave-particle relation occurs in the classical macroscopic limit, or as the mass of the quantum entity becomes infinitely large. As the mass \( m \) or velocity \( v \) of a physical body increases, its momentum \( p = mv \) grows by several orders of magnitude relative to the Planck constant. Under this macroscopic limit, the characteristic quantum wavelength vanishes, and the wave-like wavepacket size decreases below any observable scale. The mathematical link between these dual properties is formally modeled by the de Broglie relation as

\[ p = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \hbar k \]

where the high-momentum limit guarantees that the spatial wavelength \( \lambda \) approaches zero, forcing the wave function to localize into a highly focused, delta-like classical trajectory. Consequently, the highly wave-like, quantum-dominated diffraction features of the microscopic regime dissolve into the flat-space trajectories of classical mechanics, proving that the wave-particle model is compatible with classical dynamics. This seamless mathematical transition guarantees that the classical limit is recovered without any physical singularities, preserving the conceptual consistency of quantum models across all mass scales. Under this continuous reduction, the non-linear quantum wavefields contract into classical straight-line trajectories.

identities.title: De Broglie Momentum-Wavelength Relation
identities.description: The de Broglie relation links particle momentum to its corresponding spatial wavelength or wavevector, acting as the mathematical foundation of wave-particle duality.
